entries.title: MDA: players experience a designed system backwards
entries.creator: Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek
entries.sourceLabel: MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research · AAAI (2004)
entries.centralIdea: The MDA framework separates a game into Mechanics, Dynamics and Aesthetics. Mechanics are the encoded rules, actions, data and algorithms; dynamics are the behaviours that emerge when those mechanics interact with players over time; aesthetics are the desired emotional experiences—challenge, fellowship, discovery or expression, rather than merely visual style. Hunicke, LeBlanc and Zubek argue that designers usually work outward from mechanics towards experience, while players encounter the same system in reverse: first they feel the experience, then notice recurring behaviour, and only gradually infer the rules. This matters because a mechanic does not manufacture “fun” directly. It changes incentives and interactions, which may generate unexpected dynamics and therefore a different experience from the one intended. Good design moves repeatedly in both directions: trace the desired experience down to implementable rules, then test what those rules actually cause people to do and feel.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This is a compact bridge between game design, systems thinking and organisational design. It explains why a technically correct feature can still create the wrong culture or experience—and why evaluation must follow the causal chain from rules, through behaviour, to felt consequences.
entries.commonplaceEntry: People rarely experience a designed rule as a rule; they experience the behaviour it produces. A reward, constraint, ranking or default changes how participants act with one another, and that interaction creates the felt character of the system. The MDA lens therefore asks two linked questions. Working backwards: what mechanics could support the experience we want? Working forwards: what dynamics are these mechanics actually producing? The gap between those answers is where unintended consequences live. A feature can operate exactly as specified while damaging the whole. Judge a mechanism not only by its local function, but by the behaviour it invites and the experience that behaviour compounds over time.
entries.questionToCarry: What behaviour does this rule reliably invite, and is that behaviour creating the experience the system was meant to produce?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the authors’ 2004 AAAI workshop paper defines mechanics as game components at the level of data and algorithms, dynamics as run-time behaviour arising from interaction, and aesthetics as desirable emotional responses. It explicitly contrasts the designer’s mechanics-to-aesthetics perspective with the player’s reverse perspective and presents MDA as an iterative design and analysis method. The framework is influential, but the paper proposes a conceptual tool rather than reporting controlled evidence that it is uniquely correct or complete. Its list of aesthetic goals is illustrative, not a universal taxonomy. Applying MDA to organisations, interfaces or policies is an interpretive extension: the causal vocabulary transfers plausibly, but those systems have actors, power relations and goals more complex than a game.

entries.title: The fountain pen feed: a controlled leak and a controlled breath
entries.creator: Alex Nikolov, Sohail Murad, Darsh Wasan and Pingkeng Wu
entries.sourceLabel: How capillarity and ink–air flow govern a fountain pen · Journal of Colloid and Interface Science (2020)
entries.centralIdea: A fountain pen must let ink travel down to the nib while admitting air back into the reservoir, yet do neither so freely that it floods or starves. Nikolov and colleagues describe its operation as a balance between hydrostatic pressure and the holding pressure of a capillary valve. Narrow, wettable passages draw and retain ink; paper removes ink from the nib; and an air bubble enters the reservoir only when the pressure balance permits it, replacing the lost volume and restarting the cycle. The feed’s channels and collector spaces therefore do more than carry liquid: together they meter flow, buffer excess and keep ink available near the nib. Lewis Waterman’s 1896 patent already separated a capillary ink fissure from an air duct and described the flow stopping automatically when ink covered the air inlet. A fountain pen is not merely a tiny tank with a point. It is a passive feedback system built from geometry, pressure and surface chemistry.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This turns a familiar writing tool into a compact lesson in fluid mechanics and control. Its reliability comes not from maximising one flow, but from coordinating two coupled flows through carefully chosen geometry—a useful model for any design that must regulate itself without active control.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A fountain pen works because two opposing journeys are coordinated: ink moves towards the paper while air moves back towards the reservoir. The narrow ink path exploits capillarity; the air path relieves the falling pressure left behind as ink is consumed. If either route dominates, the pen floods, burps, skips or dries. Its feed is therefore a regulator rather than a pipe. No sensor or software measures the flow: channel widths, wetting, pressure thresholds and small storage spaces embody the control logic in the object itself. Good passive design often looks like this—not maximum throughput, but a geometry that makes the desired exchange easy and unstable behaviour difficult.
entries.questionToCarry: What other apparently simple tools succeed by coordinating two opposing flows rather than maximising either one?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the 2020 study identifies the balance between reservoir holding pressure and pressure across the capillary valve as central to fountain-pen function, and experimentally examines how the feed–cartridge connection affects performance. Waterman’s 1896 patent explicitly describes a capillary ink fissure, a separate duct for returning air bubbles and automatic stopping when ink closes the air inlet. A 2011 fluid-dynamics study independently shows that writing also depends on the balance between capillary driving force and resistance in the porous paper. Interpretation: calling the feed a passive feedback system, a controlled leak and a controlled breath is an engineering analogy. Feed geometries vary, and temperature, orientation, ink properties and manufacturing tolerances can disturb the balance.

entries.title: The garden of forking paths: one analysis, many unseen alternatives
entries.creator: Andrew Gelman and Eric Loken
entries.sourceLabel: The garden of forking paths · Columbia University Statistics (2013)
entries.centralIdea: An analysis can suffer from multiple comparisons even when the researcher runs only one test. Gelman and Loken’s “garden of forking paths” begins earlier: choices about exclusions, transformations, outcomes, subgroups, covariates and interactions may be made after seeing features of the data, each choice appearing defensible in context. The reported path is singular, but another dataset could have prompted another equally plausible route. Conventional significance calculations usually treat the chosen route as if it had been fixed in advance, ignoring the larger set of analyses that might have been selected. No conscious fishing or dishonesty is required; good-faith theory can rationalise the turn that looks sensible after the result is visible. The remedy is not one ritual. Preregistration separates planned from exploratory work; multiverse or specification analyses expose how conclusions vary across defensible choices; replication tests whether the selected pattern survives new data.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This names a failure mode that lives between bad statistics and bad character. It redirects scrutiny from whether an analyst intended to manipulate a result toward whether the conclusion remains stable across the reasonable decisions the data could have invited.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A result inherits uncertainty from the route used to reach it. If cleaning rules, outcomes, subgroups or model terms were chosen partly in response to the observed data, the final p-value describes only the selected path—not the garden of plausible paths surrounding it. Sincerity does not remove this multiplicity; a theoretically respectable explanation can be found for whichever turn the data makes attractive. Record decisions before outcomes are visible when confirmation matters. When several choices are genuinely defensible, show the range: rerun the analysis across them, explain which specifications are credible, and distinguish a stable conclusion from one that exists only at a convenient fork.
entries.questionToCarry: Would this conclusion survive the other defensible analytical choices I could have made at each fork?
entries.evidenceNote: Established as Gelman and Loken’s methodological argument: data-contingent researcher choices create an implicit multiple-comparisons problem even when only one analysis is executed and no deliberate p-hacking occurs. The paper illustrates the mechanism through published cases; it is not a theorem assigning a universal false-positive rate to every flexible workflow. Supporting evidence: a 2024 multiverse study of an N400 experiment found that several defensible preprocessing and measurement choices changed at least some outcomes. Limits: preregistration can clarify confirmatory claims but cannot repair weak theory, poor measurement or noisy data; multiverse analyses also require judgment about which specifications are genuinely defensible. Calling the unreported alternatives uncertainty inherited by the result is an interpretive summary.

entries.title: Luke 10: the kingdom comes near before it is welcomed
entries.creator: The Gospel according to Luke
entries.sourceLabel: Luke 10:1–12 · English Standard Version on Bible.com
entries.centralIdea: In Luke 10, Jesus appoints seventy-two others and sends them in pairs ahead of him. Their sequence matters: first ask the Lord of the harvest to send workers; then go as lambs among wolves, without the normal securities of moneybag, knapsack or sandals. They enter as guests, offer peace, accept hospitality without trading up, heal the sick and announce that God’s kingdom has come near. When a town refuses them, they withdraw and warn rather than coerce—but the announcement remains: the kingdom has still come near. Reception changes the town’s response to God’s reign; it does not manufacture that reign. The disciples are neither conquering heroes nor travelling proprietors. They are vulnerable witnesses whose fellowship, dependence, peace and healing make visible the approach of the King who sent them and is himself coming to those places.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: The passage joins mission to humility. Prayer precedes action, companions precede individual heroics, hospitality precedes proclamation, and healing embodies the message. It also prevents acceptance from becoming the measure of truth: rejection does not reverse what God is doing.
entries.commonplaceEntry: The seventy-two do not carry the kingdom as private property. They are sent ahead of Jesus to reveal that God’s reign has drawn near. Their manner is part of the message: two by two, prayerful, exposed, dependent on welcome, offering peace and healing. They cannot force reception, improve the truth by success, or cancel it by failure. If received, they remain and share the table. If rejected, they leave without coercion, yet speak the same reality: the kingdom has come near. Christian witness therefore holds confidence and powerlessness together. The messenger acts, serves and speaks clearly, while leaving both provision and response outside the messenger’s control.
entries.questionToCarry: How can a witness make the kingdom’s nearness visible without trying to control whether it is received?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by Luke 10:1–12: Jesus appoints the group, sends them two by two ahead of himself, commands prayer, describes them as lambs among wolves, removes ordinary travel provisions, tells them to offer peace, remain in one house, receive food, heal the sick and announce the kingdom’s nearness. Receptive and unreceptive towns receive the same central announcement, although rejection also brings a warning of judgment. Interpretation: saying that the mission reveals a kingdom already drawing near through Jesus, rather than producing it through acceptance, follows from that repeated announcement and from the disciples being sent where Jesus intends to come. Textual uncertainty: ancient manuscripts divide between seventy and seventy-two; the ESV prints seventy-two. Modern application beyond this particular mission is theological interpretation, not an explicit universal procedure.

additionalSources.label: Luke’s Kingdom mission in literary context · BibleProject

entries.title: How to Speak: give the audience an empowerment promise
entries.creator: Patrick Henry Winston
entries.sourceLabel: How to Speak · MIT OpenCourseWare video
entries.centralIdea: Patrick Winston treats speaking as a learnable craft: knowledge and practice matter more than an imagined gift for performance. His governing test is whether an audience can understand, retain and value an idea. Begin with an “empowerment promise”—state what listeners will be able to know or do by the end. Then cycle around the central idea, distinguish it from neighbouring ideas, and use verbal punctuation so attention can rejoin after it wanders. Match medium to purpose: Winston prefers the board for teaching because writing pace approximates absorption pace, while slides can expose material too quickly. For technical talks, situate the problem, show a vision, enumerate what has been done, and end on contributions rather than a generic thank-you slide. The deeper point is ethical as well as practical: presentation is not cosmetic packaging applied after thought. It is the engineering required for an idea to survive transmission.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: The lecture joins communication, teaching and systems thinking. Each technique has a function—orientation, pacing, recovery or memory—so style becomes inspectable rather than mystical. It is especially useful when the material is complex enough that clarity cannot be improvised.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A talk is a designed path through another person’s attention. Begin by promising a real change in what the audience will understand. Revisit the central idea from more than one angle, mark transitions aloud, and provide landmarks where a distracted listener can re-enter. Choose tools for cognitive pace, not prestige: a board can slow explanation to the speed of comprehension, while a slide can make information appear faster than it can be integrated. Finish by naming the contribution, because the final frame remains after the supporting detail fades. Good speaking is not performance layered over substance. It is the craft of carrying substance across the gap between minds with as little damage as possible.
entries.questionToCarry: What will this audience be able to understand or do after the talk that they could not do before it?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by the source: MIT OpenCourseWare identifies Patrick Henry Winston as the instructor and provides the playable lecture and transcript. The transcript explicitly recommends beginning with an “empowerment promise,” revisiting the subject, distinguishing an idea from alternatives, marking transitions, matching tools to purpose, situating technical work and closing with contributions. MIT records the talk as a long-running Institute tradition. Qualification: these are Winston’s accumulated teaching and speaking heuristics, demonstrated through the lecture itself; the source does not provide controlled evidence that each technique improves outcomes across audiences. Claims about attention, pacing and memory should therefore be treated as experienced guidance, sensitive to accessibility needs, format and context. Describing presentation as transmission engineering is an interpretation of the lecture.

entries.title: The Byzantine Generals Problem: agreement when messages may lie
entries.creator: Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak and Marshall Pease
entries.sourceLabel: The Byzantine Generals Problem · ACM TOPLAS (1982)
entries.centralIdea: In a distributed system, failure is not always silence. A faulty component may tell one peer “attack” and another “retreat,” leaving honest participants with incompatible views. Lamport, Shostak and Pease modelled this as generals who must agree on a plan despite traitors. Their two requirements are stricter than majority voting: loyal participants must reach the same decision, and if the commander is loyal, they must follow the commander’s order. Under their “oral messages” assumptions—messages arrive, sender identity is known, but content can be fabricated by a faulty sender—agreement tolerating m traitors requires at least 3m+1 participants. With unforgeable signed messages, the bound changes dramatically. The lasting insight is architectural: trustworthiness is not a property of individual messages alone. It emerges from redundancy, authenticated communication, explicit fault assumptions and an agreement procedure designed for the worst behaviour the system permits.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This is the mathematics beneath fault-tolerant databases, replicated services and some consensus systems. More broadly, it separates ordinary error from adversarial inconsistency: checking one report is insufficient when a source can present different realities to different observers.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Consensus is easy when failure means silence; harder when failure can imitate confidence and contradict itself. The Byzantine Generals Problem asks honest participants to agree even when some nodes tell different stories to different listeners. Its lesson is not simply “trust nobody.” Agreement requires a declared failure model. How many actors may be faulty? Can identities be forged? Do messages arrive within known bounds? Are signatures reliable? The answers determine what guarantees are possible and how much redundancy is required. Robust systems do not rely on sincerity as an unstated assumption. They specify the kinds of deception or malfunction they must survive, then build enough verification, replication and communication to make agreement defensible.
entries.questionToCarry: Which failure modes does this system actually tolerate, and which ones has it merely assumed away?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by the 1982 paper: in its oral-message model, agreement is solvable if and only if more than two-thirds of the generals are loyal; tolerating m traitors therefore requires at least 3m+1 participants. With the paper’s unforgeable signed-message assumptions, the problem is solvable regardless of the number of traitors, subject to the stated communication and connectivity conditions. These are formal results inside explicit models: oral messages assume correct delivery from loyal senders, identifiable senders and detectable absence; signed messages assume signatures cannot be forged or altered undetected. Modern systems may also face asynchronous delivery, compromised keys, network partitions or changing membership. The theorem does not by itself certify any database or blockchain implementation. Extending the lesson to human organisations is interpretive analogy.

entries.title: Braess’s paradox: when a new road makes every journey slower
entries.creator: Dietrich Braess
entries.sourceLabel: On a Paradox of Traffic Planning · Transportation Science
entries.centralIdea: Dietrich Braess showed that more capacity need not mean better performance when users independently choose the quickest route. In his constructed network, two routes initially divide traffic. Add a fast connector and each driver has an incentive to use it; those individually sensible switches load the same congestion-sensitive links. At the new equilibrium no one can improve by changing route alone, yet everyone travels more slowly than before. The road has not physically harmed the network. It has changed the incentives governing how the network is used. This is an instance of the “price of anarchy”: decentralized optimisation can settle at a state worse than coordinated allocation. Removing, restricting or pricing a link can therefore improve total flow—but only where topology, demand and delay functions create the required structure. The paradox is not that roads are bad. It is that options alter behaviour, and local improvement does not necessarily compose into system improvement.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This turns infrastructure design into game theory. A lane, workflow, dashboard or shortcut may be locally attractive yet systemically harmful after everyone adapts to it. The correct comparison is not capacity before behaviour changes, but the equilibrium reached afterwards.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Adding a choice changes more than the menu; it changes the game. Braess’s paradox shows a network in which a fast new link attracts rational users onto the same congestion-sensitive edges. No individual can improve by deviating from the resulting equilibrium, yet every journey is slower than it was without the link. The design error is judging a resource in isolation. Its value depends on the behaviour it induces across the whole system. Before adding a shortcut, permission or channel, ask what happens if everyone follows the incentive it creates. Sometimes subtraction, friction or coordination raises total performance—not because less is inherently better, but because the unmanaged equilibrium was the bottleneck.
entries.questionToCarry: If everyone adopts the locally best response to this new option, what equilibrium does the whole system settle into?
entries.evidenceNote: Established mathematically: Braess’s 1968 paper constructs road-network conditions under which adding a link redistributes user-optimised flow and raises individual travel times; INFORMS published an English translation in 2005. Stanford lecture notes show that the canonical affine-cost augmented network has a price of anarchy of 4/3. Evidence beyond the toy network: a 2008 Physical Review Letters simulation of several major-city road networks found that blocking selected streets could improve modelled traffic conditions. Qualification: this is simulation and model evidence, not proof of a universal field effect. The paradox depends on network topology, fixed or modelled demand, congestion-sensitive delay functions and route-choice assumptions; most added capacity need not worsen performance. Applying the result to organisational workflows or dashboards is an interpretive analogy.

additionalSources.label: Selfish Routing and the Price of Anarchy · Stanford CS364A lecture notes

entries.title: The repeated-bout effect: why the second shock lands softer
entries.creator: Robert D. Hyldahl, Trevor C. Chen and Kazunori Nosaka
entries.sourceLabel: Mechanisms and Mediators of the Skeletal Muscle Repeated Bout Effect · Exercise and Sport Sciences Reviews
entries.centralIdea: Unfamiliar eccentric exercise—producing force while a muscle lengthens, as when lowering a weight or walking downhill—can cause temporary strength loss, soreness and other markers of muscle damage. Repeat a similar bout later and the disturbance is usually smaller: the repeated-bout effect. Remarkably, one exposure can begin this protection. It is not merely increased pain tolerance. Studies report attenuated soreness, swelling and blood markers, with faster recovery of strength and range of motion. No single mechanism explains it. Reviews point to interacting neural changes, altered mechanical properties, remodelling of muscle and extracellular matrix, and modified inflammatory signalling. The adaptation is specific enough that a radically different task may not inherit the same protection, yet broad enough to show that muscle does more than rebuild what was disrupted: it changes how later stress is distributed and repaired. The first bout is therefore information as well as load.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: It is a concrete example of biological learning: exposure changes not only capacity but the cost of repeating the same stress. It also explains why an unfamiliar session can feel disproportionately punishing without proving that the session was unusually productive.
entries.commonplaceEntry: The body can become more resistant to a stress after meeting it once. In the repeated-bout effect, the same eccentric work produces less disruption on later exposure because muscle, connective structure, neural recruitment and inflammatory signalling have adapted together. The useful lesson is not to chase damage. Soreness is an imperfect signal, and reduced soreness does not mean that training has stopped working. Adaptation often looks like the disappearance of the very disturbance that first made progress visible. A system may be improving when the same input causes less chaos, quicker recovery and better preserved function. Measure capability and recovery, not merely how dramatic the stress felt.
entries.questionToCarry: Where am I mistaking a smaller disturbance on repetition for a weaker stimulus rather than evidence that the system has adapted?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: repeated similar eccentric exercise usually produces less soreness, swelling and leakage of muscle proteins into blood, with smaller losses of strength and range of motion—the repeated-bout effect. Reviews group proposed explanations into neural, mechanical and cellular adaptations; later work emphasises that extracellular-matrix remodelling and biochemical or inflammatory signalling probably interact with them. Uncertain: there is no single accepted mechanism, and the relative contribution of each pathway varies with the protocol. Limits: the strongest evidence concerns eccentric, muscle-damaging exercise; protection depends on the similarity, timing and intensity of later work and is not immunity from strain or injury. “Biological learning” and the wider systems analogy are interpretations.

additionalSources.label: Foundational synthesis of neural, mechanical and cellular explanations · Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports

entries.title: The dollar auction: when quitting costs more than continuing
entries.creator: Martin Shubik
entries.sourceLabel: The Dollar Auction Game · Journal of Conflict Resolution (1971)
entries.centralIdea: In Martin Shubik’s dollar auction, a dollar bill goes to the highest bidder, but the highest and second-highest bidders must both pay their final bids. Entry looks cheap. Once two players remain, each faces an ugly comparison: quit and crystallise a loss, or bid slightly more for a chance to win and reduce it. When bids approach or exceed the prize, continuing can still look locally preferable even though the joint outcome keeps worsening. The game compresses escalation of commitment, competition and irrecoverable cost into a few rules. It should not be misread as proof that fully rational players must spiral forever: later formal analysis shows that, with specified budgets and assumptions, strategic players can avoid the contest. Its lasting force is structural. A sequence of individually defensible next steps can carry participants far beyond a boundary they would have rejected before the first bid.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This tiny game illuminates project overruns, bidding wars, arms races and arguments pursued chiefly because conceding now feels worse than paying once more. It separates the rationality of the next move from the rationality of the path.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Escalation survives by changing the comparison. Before entering, the question is whether the prize justifies the contest. After losses accumulate, the question becomes whether one more payment is cheaper than admitting defeat. That narrower calculation can be locally coherent while the total position becomes absurd. Sunk cost matters strategically when an opponent knows that withdrawal is painful, but it should not be mistaken for value. A useful reset is to erase the history temporarily: if I owned none of the prior bids, would I enter this exact game now, at this price, under these rules? If not, continuing needs a reason stronger than the desire to make the past come out differently.
entries.questionToCarry: If I had made none of the previous bids, would I willingly enter this contest at its current position?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: Shubik’s 1971 game awards the dollar to the highest bidder while requiring both the highest and second-highest bidders to pay; he presented it as a simple experimental model of escalation. Qualification: the auction is not an inescapable theorem of irrationality. Barry O’Neill’s 1986 finite-budget analysis derived strategies under which rational players avoid bidding against one another and argued that the game exploits some irrationality rather than forming an innate trap. Behavioural evidence remains strong: three 2018 experiments involving 1,229 participants found that most people, including experienced managers, escalated without intervention. Direct experience with structurally similar escalation and observing others’ consequences reduced later escalation; a pre-set exit-limit intervention did not. Applying the game to projects, conflict or relationships is analogical because their payoffs, information and stopping rules are less clean.

additionalSources.label: Competitive escalation and interventions · Journal of Behavioral Decision Making (2018)

entries.title: The Kuleshov effect: meaning is made in the cut
entries.creator: Lev Kuleshov
entries.sourceLabel: Kuleshov on Film · University of California Press
entries.centralIdea: Lev Kuleshov’s classic demonstration intercut the same neutral face with different images—traditionally soup, a coffin and a pleasant scene. Viewers reportedly credited actor Ivan Mozzhukhin with hunger, grief or warmth, though his shot never changed. The creative claim is larger than facial expression: a shot does not carry meaning alone. The viewer builds a relationship across the cut, inferring gaze, cause, intention and emotion. Modern experiments support a contextual effect, but not the strongest textbook myth. The original footage is lost, its controls and statistics absent, and replications have varied. Better-controlled studies nevertheless find that adjoining emotional scenes shift valence and category judgments of neutral faces; recent work using authentic film sequences also reports behavioural and neural differences. Editing therefore does not magically override performance. It supplies a frame within which an ambiguous performance is interpreted.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: Film technique becomes a lesson in cognition and communication: context is not decoration around evidence. The sequence in which information arrives can change the meaning a viewer constructs from material that has not itself changed.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A neutral face is not read neutrally. Place it beside food and the viewer may infer hunger; beside loss, grief. The cut invites the mind to invent a relationship between separate images, supplying intention and emotion that neither shot contains by itself. This does not mean context can make anything mean anything, or that performance is irrelevant. It means interpretation is relational. Order, adjacency and implied point of view act upon the evidence. Whenever an image, quotation or number appears self-explanatory, inspect its neighbouring shot: what came immediately before, what was withheld, and what connection has the sequence encouraged the audience to manufacture?
entries.questionToCarry: What meaning am I attributing to this evidence because of the material placed immediately before or after it?
entries.evidenceNote: Established historically: Kuleshov developed montage experiments in which identical shots of a neutral face were juxtaposed with different scenes to evoke different interpretations. Uncertainty: the original footage is lost, the demonstrations lacked modern controls and statistical analysis, and later replications have produced mixed results. A 2016 behavioural and eye-tracking study found context-congruent shifts in emotion categorisation, valence and arousal, but described the result cautiously as “some sort” of Kuleshov effect. A 2024 study using newly filmed face–scene–face sequences reported strong contextual effects on valence plus associated fMRI differences, while finding no change in one measure of perceived emotional intensity. Interpretation: applying the effect to quotations, numbers or general communication is an analogy; the empirical studies concern film sequences and facial-emotion judgments.

additionalSources.label: Controlled replication · Perception (2016)

entries.title: Ecclesiastes 11: sow because you do not know
entries.creator: The Book of Ecclesiastes
entries.sourceLabel: Ecclesiastes 11:1–6 · English Standard Version on Bible.com
entries.centralIdea: Ecclesiastes 11:1–6 repeats one hard fact: you do not know. You do not know what disaster may occur, how life forms in the womb, or which sowing will prosper. Yet the Teacher’s answer is not retreat. Bread is sent on waters, portions are divided among seven or eight, and seed is sown morning and evening. The watcher who waits for perfect wind never sows. Interpretations of the opening images vary—generosity, trade and agriculture are all defended—so the passage is not a simple investment manual. Its coherent movement is from uncertainty to distributed, persistent action. Human beings cannot master God’s work or secure the future; they can refuse to let incomplete knowledge become paralysis. Wisdom here is neither certainty nor recklessness. It is acting within creaturely limits: spread exposure, keep working, accept that outcomes remain contingent, and leave room for more than one effort to prosper.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This is a rare meeting of theology and decision theory. The text neither promises control nor glorifies ignorance; it treats diversification and continued action as sensible responses to a world whose outcomes remain partly hidden.
entries.commonplaceEntry: “You do not know” is not Ecclesiastes’ argument for doing nothing. It is the reason to sow again, to avoid resting everything on one outcome and to stop waiting for conditions without risk. Perfect foresight is unavailable; responsible action is still possible. The passage does not guarantee that diligence will produce the preferred result, nor does it baptise every gamble as faith. It locates wisdom between control and paralysis: act with what can be known, distribute what can be lost, continue the work, and receive the outcome without pretending it was ever fully yours to command. Creaturely limitation is not failure. It is the truthful boundary within which faithfulness operates.
entries.questionToCarry: Where am I treating the absence of certainty as permission not to sow at all?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by the text: Ecclesiastes 11:1–6 repeatedly states that the reader does not know future disaster, God’s work or which sowing will succeed; it nevertheless commands giving portions, sowing and not withholding the hand. Verse 4 explicitly warns that watching wind and clouds can prevent action. Interpretive uncertainty: “cast your bread upon the waters” has been read as generosity, maritime trade or agricultural imagery, and the precise relationship among verses 1–2 remains debated. Christopher Whitwell argues that variation in nature links the passage and that repeated sowing reduces risk. Theological interpretation: describing this as faithful action within creaturely limits draws on verse 5 and the book’s wider concern with limited control; the text does not promise that diversification or diligence guarantees success.

entries.title: The hot hand’s hidden denominator: when a fair coin looks anti-streaky
entries.creator: Joshua B. Miller and Adam Sanjurjo
entries.sourceLabel: Surprised by the Hot Hand Fallacy? · Econometrica (2018)
entries.centralIdea: Miller and Sanjurjo found a selection bias in a familiar streak test. Suppose a fair coin is flipped three times. Within each sequence, record the proportion of heads among flips immediately following a head, discarding sequences with no eligible flip. The average of those sequence-level proportions is not one-half but 5/12. The conditioning rule changes the sample: the result used to identify an eligible position also constrains the finite sequence being measured, while overlapping streaks intensify the effect. The bias shrinks as sequences lengthen but grows with the chosen streak length. This mattered because classic hot-hand studies compared basketball shooting after runs of hits using a downward-biased measure, making positive dependence look smaller or absent. After correcting it and re-analysing the original data, the authors found significant evidence of streak shooting. A neutral process can look anti-streaky when the observation rule quietly manufactures its own baseline.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: It is a compact warning for data work and sport alike: conditioning can change the expected value before any real effect appears. A denominator may look innocent while encoding the very selection process the analysis is meant to test.
entries.commonplaceEntry: The dataset does not begin after collection; it begins when a rule decides which observations count. In streak analysis, selecting only outcomes that follow prior successes creates a finite-sample baseline below the underlying success rate. Compare the observed result with one-half and real persistence can disappear. The error is subtle because every included observation is genuine—the distortion lives in eligibility and averaging, not fabrication. Before interpreting a conditional percentage, ask what had to happen for an observation to enter its denominator, what sequences were excluded, and what the estimator would report under a neutral process. A fair comparison requires the null distribution of the procedure, not merely the intuitive baseline of the phenomenon.
entries.questionToCarry: What would this selection-and-averaging rule report if the underlying process contained no effect at all?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: Miller and Sanjurjo prove that, for finite independent binary sequences, the within-sequence proportion of successes immediately following a success streak is downward-biased; for three fair flips after one head, its conditional expectation is 5/12 rather than one-half. They show that the bias generally falls with sequence length and rises with streak length. Their bias-corrected reanalysis of the 1985 Gilovich–Vallone–Tversky shooting data found significant streak effects with large estimated magnitudes. Qualification: this overturns the claim that the original analysis established a universal hot-hand fallacy; it does not prove that every observed run is a changing performance state, nor that observers judge streaks accurately. Interpretation: treating denominator design as the wider lesson is an analytical generalisation from the theorem.

entries.title: Negative capability: resisting premature certainty
entries.creator: John Keats
entries.sourceLabel: The negative capability letter · Mapping Keats’s Progress
entries.centralIdea: John Keats coined “negative capability” in an 1817 letter while asking what enabled Shakespearean achievement. He valued the capacity to remain with uncertainty, mystery and incomplete knowledge without rushing to force a conclusion. In its original setting this is an artistic quality: the poet does not flatten experience into a single explanatory system before its contradictions have done their work. The idea need not oppose evidence or reason. A useful modern reading is temporal: reason has a proper moment, but premature closure can destroy information, imagination and alternative hypotheses. Negative capability is therefore not passive indecision. It is disciplined suspension—holding several live possibilities, observing what each explains, and delaying commitment until the evidence or the work genuinely requires it. The difficult skill is distinguishing uncertainty that should be investigated from uncertainty that should not yet be eliminated.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This joins creativity with rigorous judgement: poets and analysts alike can damage reality by resolving ambiguity too quickly. It names the patience required to let a pattern emerge without mistaking discomfort for a demand to decide.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Not every uncertainty is a defect in the model; sometimes it is faithful representation of the situation. Negative capability means resisting the emotional pressure to close a question before its evidence has matured. The discipline is not to celebrate vagueness, but to keep rival explanations alive long enough to learn what each reveals. A rushed answer may feel cleaner while discarding the very tension that contains the insight. Remain open, gather detail, and decide when action truly requires decision. Intellectual maturity includes both powers: the courage to conclude and the restraint to leave a question unresolved when certainty would be counterfeit.
entries.questionToCarry: Which uncertainty am I trying to eliminate because it is uncomfortable rather than because the evidence now supports a conclusion?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the phrase appears in the surviving transcript tradition of Keats’s December 1817 letter to his brothers George and Tom, where it concerns literary achievement and Shakespeare. Interpretation: applying it to analysis, decisions and hypothesis management extends beyond Keats’s explicit argument. Uncertainty: the letter is conventionally dated 21 and possibly 27 December. Cambridge scholarship notes that the wording reaches us through John Jeffrey’s 1845 transcript rather than a surviving autograph; comparisons with Jeffrey’s other transcripts show that he could alter or omit material. The precise wording should therefore not be treated as an unquestionable manuscript reading, and the concept supplies no rule for how long judgement should be suspended.

additionalSources.label: Textual history of the surviving transcript · Cambridge University Press

entries.title: The co-axial escapement: redesign the contact, not the lubricant
entries.creator: George Daniels
entries.sourceLabel: George Daniels’s escapement patent · EP0018796B1
entries.centralIdea: A mechanical watch’s escapement repeatedly locks and releases the gear train while giving the balance wheel tiny impulses. In the conventional lever escapement, inclined pallet surfaces help perform both locking and impulsing, producing sliding contact that depends on lubrication. George Daniels changed the geometry and separated those functions. His patented arrangement uses distinct locking and impulse pallets, with concentric rings of escape-wheel teeth operating in parallel planes. On alternating swings, one impulse reaches the balance directly and the other passes through the lever; the impulse faces are arranged radially and their contact areas kept small. The aim was not stronger oil but far less need for oil at the critical interface. This preserved the practical virtues of a wristwatch escapement—bidirectional impulse and self-starting—while attacking a source of friction, lubricant ageing and rate instability through architecture.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: It is miniature systems engineering expressed in metal: one troublesome interface was decomposed into separate responsibilities. The lesson travels well—when maintenance remains stubborn, inspect whether a component is being asked to perform conflicting functions.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Daniels’s co-axial escapement is a lesson in removing a problem at the level of geometry. Traditional escapements tolerated sliding friction and managed it with lubricant. Daniels asked whether locking and energy transfer had been bundled into the same contact unnecessarily. By separating them and redirecting the impulse, he reduced dependence on that sliding interface. The general principle is powerful: recurring maintenance may be evidence not of inadequate upkeep, but of an architecture that continually recreates the fault. Before optimising the oil, schedule or workaround, inspect the contact itself. A durable design often emerges when restraint, transmission and release are each given a form suited to their own job.
entries.questionToCarry: Which recurring maintenance problem exists because one interface is being asked both to restrain movement and transmit energy?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by Daniels’s European patent: the design separates locking and impulsing, applies alternating impulses directly and through the lever, uses radial impulse surfaces, remains self-starting and was intended to avoid pallet lubrication. The Science Museum describes its working model as having virtually no sliding friction and requiring minimal lubrication; Omega began series use in 1999. Qualification: “co-axial” does not mean an entire watch runs without friction or oil, and production implementations differ from the patent embodiments. Omega’s claims of longer servicing needs and greater long-term precision are manufacturer claims rather than proof that the escapement alone causes every reported benefit. Interpretation: treating the mechanism as a general lesson in separating conflicting functions is an engineering analogy.

entries.title: John Locke’s two-page index for a growing commonplace book
entries.creator: John Locke
entries.sourceLabel: A New Method of Making Common-Place-Books · 1706 edition scan
entries.centralIdea: A bound notebook creates a stubborn information problem: topics grow unpredictably, but its pages cannot be rearranged. John Locke’s method avoided reserving wasteful blocks for subjects. He placed a compact grid at the front, combining each initial letter with the first vowel that followed it in a chosen heading. A note headed “Epistola,” for example, belonged under E–i. That cell recorded the page where the heading began; if its page filled, the subject continued on the next available blank page and the index gained another pointer. Notes could therefore be written into available space while remaining recoverable by topic. The important invention is architectural rather than merely alphabetical: capture order and retrieval order are separated. A small, stable index can govern a body of notes whose subjects, proportions and connections cannot be predicted in advance.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: Locke’s notebook behaves like a tiny analogue database: sparse index, dynamic allocation and pointers to distributed records. It shows that useful knowledge systems need not predict future categories perfectly; they need a dependable route back.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A commonplace book becomes valuable only when an earlier thought can be recovered at the moment it matters. Locke’s answer was not to perfect the taxonomy before writing. He let notes occupy the next useful space, then maintained a compact index that pointed to them. The durable principle is separation: storage may be chronological or opportunistic while retrieval remains topical. This reduces the penalty for guessing wrong about how much room a subject deserves. Yet an indexing system must remain lighter than the practice it supports. The best structure is not the most ingenious one; it is the smallest one that future-you will actually maintain and trust.
entries.questionToCarry: What is the smallest index that would let a future reader recover this note without remembering when or where it was written?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the surviving 1706 English edition contains a two-page index and explains classification by a heading’s initial letter and first following vowel, with page references for later retrieval. The edition is a posthumous English translation of Locke’s earlier method. Historical scholarship places it within existing systematic, alphabetical and sequential commonplacing traditions, so “invention” should not imply creation from nothing; Locke’s contribution was a flexible synthesis refined through long use. Harvard’s example of a later Locke-style notebook also shows that users did not always follow or maintain the scheme. Interpretation: describing the system as analogue database architecture is a modern analogy, and its practical superiority depends on the keeper’s habits.

entries.title: The illusion of explanatory depth: explanation as a confidence test
entries.creator: Leonid Rozenblit and Frank Keil
entries.sourceLabel: The misunderstood limits of folk science · Cognitive Science (2002)
entries.centralIdea: Recognising a system is not the same as possessing a causal model of it. Rozenblit and Keil asked participants to rate how well they understood familiar devices, attempt detailed step-by-step explanations, answer mechanism questions and then rate themselves again. Confidence fell after the attempt to explain. The effect was strongest for causally complex devices and natural phenomena, and weaker for facts, procedures and narratives. Visible parts, familiar labels and easy access to information may create a feeling of understanding that is mistaken for an explanation held in the mind. The practical test is generative rather than recognitional: before trusting confidence, try to state each causal step, identify what triggers the next one and mark every missing link. Explanation turns a comfortable impression into something inspectable—and exposes precisely where learning must begin.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: It offers a compact bridge between learning, analysis and intellectual humility. Asking for a mechanism is more diagnostic than asking whether something “makes sense,” because fluent recognition can survive while genuine understanding is absent.
entries.commonplaceEntry: The feeling that an idea makes sense is weak evidence that I understand it. Familiar vocabulary, visible components and an available expert community can all be borrowed as if their knowledge were already mine. A better calibration test is simple: explain the mechanism without hiding behind a label. What happens first? What causes the next step? Which claim connects the stages? Where does prediction become guesswork? Failure here is useful; it converts undifferentiated confidence into a map of specific ignorance. The aim is not permanent self-doubt. It is confidence that has survived an attempt to generate the explanation, rather than confidence produced merely by recognising its parts.
entries.questionToCarry: If I had to explain this step by step without using its usual labels, where would my account first become vague?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the 2002 paper reports twelve studies and found that attempts to explain familiar mechanisms reduced participants’ self-rated understanding; the effect differed across knowledge domains. The authors also compared later ratings with independent judgements and argued that the shift reflected improved calibration. Limits: much of the evidence relies on self-ratings and convenience samples, and a later study notes that participants may partly change what they mean by “understanding” after being asked for a causal chain. That study also says the duration of the debiasing effect remains unclear. Interpretation: using step-by-step explanation as a practical confidence test is a reasonable application of the findings, not proof that every failed explanation reveals false belief.

entries.title: Wood never stops moving: designing with the grain
entries.creator: USDA Forest Products Laboratory
entries.sourceLabel: Wood Handbook, Chapter 4 · Moisture relations and physical properties of wood
entries.centralIdea: Wood is not inert stock but a humidity-responsive biological composite. It is hygroscopic: it exchanges moisture with the surrounding air, tending toward an equilibrium set largely by relative humidity and temperature. As moisture changes, wood does not move equally in every direction. From green to oven-dry, the Forest Products Laboratory gives typical shrinkage ranges of only 0.1–0.2% along the grain, 2–6% radially across growth rings, and 7–12% tangentially along them. That asymmetry explains why ring orientation can turn an invisible moisture change into cupping, gaps or split joints. Durable craft therefore does not try to overpower wood with more glue or rigidity. It uses grain orientation and joinery that restrain where necessary while allowing predictable movement elsewhere. The deeper principle is elegant: longevity often comes from respecting a material’s permitted degrees of freedom.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This turns an everyday material into an exercise in geometry, measurement and humility. A board carries the history of a cylinder, and good design succeeds by reading that hidden structure rather than treating every direction as equivalent.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Wood remembers that it was once a tree. Even after drying and machining, it continues exchanging moisture with the air, and its growth-ring geometry determines how it responds. Movement along the grain is small; movement across it is larger and unequal. This is why a broad board may cup while barely changing length, and why traditional frame-and-panel construction lets a panel float instead of pinning it rigidly. The craft lesson reaches beyond timber: do not demand stillness from a material whose nature includes movement. Identify the directions in which change will occur, constrain only what must be constrained, and give the rest somewhere harmless to go.
entries.questionToCarry: Where am I treating a predictable degree of movement as a defect, when the better design would accommodate it?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: the Forest Products Laboratory describes wood as hygroscopic and reports typical green-to-oven-dry shrinkage of 0.1–0.2% longitudinally, 2–6% radially and 7–12% tangentially. It also notes that moisture exchange depends on relative humidity, temperature and current moisture content. Values vary by species, density, board geometry, drying history and conditions; green-to-oven-dry ranges are not the same as ordinary seasonal movement in a finished object. Interpretation: the claim that durable design should provide controlled freedom is a craft principle inferred from the documented material behaviour, not a universal engineering rule.

entries.title: Psalm 13: lament is faith without camouflage
entries.creator: The Book of Psalms
entries.sourceLabel: Psalm 13 · English Standard Version on Bible.com
entries.centralIdea: Psalm 13 begins with four repetitions of “How long?” The speaker does not disguise the felt absence of God, inner sorrow or external threat. The poem then moves from complaint in verses 1–2, to a direct petition in verses 3–4, and finally to trust and promised praise in verses 5–6. Crucially, the text does not report that the circumstances changed between those movements. The change happens within the prayer: suffering is named, help is requested, and trust is placed in God’s steadfast love without pretending the pain was unreal. Lament is therefore not the opposite of faith. It is faith refusing both silence and performance—continuing to address God honestly when easy reassurance would be false. The psalm permits anguish to speak while denying it the final word.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: The psalm offers a disciplined pattern for truthful thought as well as prayer: describe reality without euphemism, ask plainly for what is needed, then decide what deeper truth current conditions cannot cancel. It avoids both forced positivity and hopelessness.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Biblical lament is faith speaking without camouflage. Psalm 13 does not begin by minimising absence; it addresses God, names sorrow and asks for an answer. Its closing trust is not supported by a narrated rescue. Trust, then, is not pretending the circumstances have changed. It is refusing to let present experience exhaust what can truthfully be said of God. Complaint, petition, trust and praise belong inside one honest prayer. The lesson is not that pain must quickly resolve into cheerfulness, but that pain may be brought into relationship rather than hidden. Lament remains prayer because it continues addressing God when silence feels more plausible.
entries.questionToCarry: What would change if truthful complaint were treated as an act of faith rather than evidence that faith is failing?
entries.evidenceNote: Established by the text: Psalm 13 repeats “How long?”, petitions God to answer, then declares trust and intended praise. The psalm supplies no historical setting beyond its attribution to David and does not narrate an external change before the closing declaration. Interpretation: describing the sequence as complaint, petition, trust and praise is a literary reading; describing the internal shift as trust without denial is an inference from that sequence. BibleProject places lament and praise within the broader design of Psalms and argues that biblical prayer neither ignores pain nor lets pain determine life’s meaning.

additionalSources.label: Psalms guide · BibleProject

entries.title: Seeing Like a State: How Certain Schemes to Improve the Human Condition Have Failed
entries.creator: James C. Scott
entries.sourceLabel: Yale University Press book page
entries.centralIdea: James C. Scott argues that large institutions cannot act on a complex society until they render it legible: standard names, cadastral maps, uniform measures, simplified forests and planned cities. Legibility creates administrative power and can deliver real benefits, but it also discards tacit relationships and local skills—what Scott calls mētis. Disaster becomes likely when four features combine: administrative simplification, high-modernist confidence, coercive power and weak civil society. The deeper lesson is not that planning or measurement is inherently wrong. It is that a representation designed for control can be mistaken for the thing represented. A clean schema may reveal patterns while hiding the dependencies that keep a system alive. Good governance therefore needs feedback, reversibility, local knowledge and the humility to treat the map as an instrument, not reality itself.
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: This is a bridge between data, organisational design, leadership and political philosophy. It explains why a technically tidy system can become less truthful as it becomes easier to administer—and why the people closest to the work often hold knowledge that no central dashboard has captured.
entries.commonplaceEntry: Legibility is useful, but it is never neutral. To manage a forest, city, organisation or population from the centre, we simplify it into categories that can be counted and compared. The resulting map may be accurate for its purpose while still omitting the relationships that make the real system function. Failure begins when the map is mistaken for reality and local knowledge is treated as noise. The corrective is not to reject standards or planning, but to combine them with practical knowledge, dissent, feedback and reversible experiments. A good system should remain governable without making reality disappear merely because reality is awkward to encode.
entries.questionToCarry: What valuable local knowledge becomes invisible when a system is redesigned to be clean, comparable and centrally manageable?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: Yale University Press identifies Scott’s book and summarises its comparative case against authoritarian high-modernist planning, including four recurring conditions in planning disasters. Those conditions are Scott’s argued framework, not a universal causal law. A scholarly counterpoint from anthropologist Michael Herzfeld says Scott overgeneralises resistance, understates how bureaucrats and local populations modify schemes together, and lacks ethnographic specificity. The safest use is therefore as a diagnostic lens, not proof that central coordination must fail.

entries.title: Why does mathematics fit the world so well?
entries.creator: Eugene P. Wigner
entries.sourceLabel: Wigner’s 1960 essay in Communications on Pure and Applied Mathematics
entries.centralIdea: In 1960, physicist Eugene Wigner asked why mathematical structures so often describe nature with precision far beyond their origins. Concepts such as complex numbers, linear operators and matrix algebra were developed largely through internal mathematical questions and aesthetic judgement; later they became indispensable in physics. For Wigner, the puzzle is not merely that calculation is useful. It is that compact abstractions can expose regularities, unify apparently different phenomena and sometimes predict features of the world before observation catches up. The essay does not settle whether mathematics is discovered, invented, selected from many failed formalisms, or effective because science focuses on mathematically tractable aspects of reality. Its lasting value is the question itself: when a model works remarkably well, what exactly is doing the work—the structure of nature, the architecture of human thought, or the disciplined selection of useful representations?
entries.whyItMayInterestYou: It connects mathematics, modelling, data and philosophy. The practical sting is that model accuracy is never merely technical: choosing an abstraction determines what can be seen, predicted and ignored. Wigner’s puzzle invites both wonder at elegant structure and suspicion toward models that look mathematically impressive without earning contact with reality.
entries.commonplaceEntry: A mathematical model is a wager that some structure matters more than the surrounding detail. Its success can be astonishing: an abstraction invented for elegance may later describe the physical world with extraordinary precision. But predictive success alone does not tell us why the fit exists. Perhaps nature is deeply mathematical; perhaps human minds and scientific methods select the small part of reality that yields to mathematics; perhaps both are true. The proper response is neither blind reverence nor cynicism. Use mathematics boldly, then keep asking which features of reality were preserved, which were discarded, and whether the model still works beyond the conditions that made it look convincing.
entries.questionToCarry: When a model predicts well, how can we tell whether it has captured a real structure rather than merely fitted the slice of reality we chose to measure?
entries.evidenceNote: Established: Wiley records the work as Wigner’s Richard Courant lecture, delivered at New York University on 11 May 1959 and published in February 1960, pages 1–14. Wigner gives historical examples and frames mathematical applicability as a puzzle. Interpretive: applying that puzzle to data and organisational models is an analogy, not Wigner’s demonstrated result. Uncertain: there is no agreed philosophical explanation; realist, structuralist, instrumentalist and selection-effect accounts remain contested.
